title: Short Stuff: Did a shipwreck double the size of the United States?
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1784 sinking of the El Cazador (also called The Hunter) carrying about nineteen tons of Spanish silver coins bound for New Orleans. The hosts recount how Jerry Murphy's 1993 trawl in the Gulf of Mexico recovered fused silver coins, then trace the context: Spain's ownership of Louisiana via the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, New Orleans' value as a port, Napoleon's reacquisition of Louisiana through the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800), the Haitian Revolution's disruption of French plans, and the 1803 sale of Louisiana to the United States for fifteen million dollars negotiated by James Monroe. They conclude that without the shipwreck, Spain might have kept its Louisiana holdings, based on a article by Kristin Conger.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the short stuff and ask each other who wrote the article being covered.

segments.title: Praise for Kristin Conger's article
segments.summary: The hosts praise former colleague Kristin Conger's article and mention her podcast Unladylike and her book.

segments.title: Jerry Murphy's 1993 find and the El Cazador
segments.summary: Fisherman Jerry Murphy trawled up fused silver coins in the Gulf of Mexico in 1993. Experts identified them as from the El Cazador (The Hunter), which vanished in 1784 after leaving Veracruz with nineteen tons of Spanish silver coin.

segments.title: Why Spain was shipping silver to New Orleans
segments.summary: The silver was headed to New Orleans, then under Spanish rule, to pay soldiers and officials after local currency was devalued and counterfeited.

segments.title: Spain's acquisition of Louisiana and New Orleans' value
segments.summary: King Louis XV ceded Louisiana to his cousin King Carlos III of Spain through the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau to keep it from the British. New Orleans was valuable as a Mississippi River port.

segments.title: Aside on New Orleans the city
segments.summary: Hosts reminisce about New Orleans and its hospitality.

segments.title: Mosquitoes, disease, and Napoleon's interest
segments.summary: New Orleans had disease problems but was valuable real estate. Napoleon, in power by 1799, wanted control of the port.

segments.title: Treaty of San Ildefonso
segments.summary: Napoleon got Spain to return Louisiana to France in exchange for giving the throne of Tuscany to Spain's son-in-law.

segments.title: Haitian Revolution disrupts French plans
segments.summary: Saint-Domingue's sugar and coffee production was central to French plans, but the enslaved population's revolt, described as the only really successful slave revolt in history, undermined them. Napoleon, facing British threats and needing money, decided to sell Louisiana.

segments.title: Louisiana Purchase negotiation
segments.summary: Thomas Jefferson sent James Monroe to buy New Orleans for about three million dollars. Napoleon countered by offering all of Louisiana for fifteen million dollars, which Monroe accepted.

segments.title: Shipwreck's hypothetical effect on history
segments.summary: The hosts say the Louisiana Purchase roughly doubled U.S. territory and reason that had the shipwreck not occurred, Spain might have kept delivering silver and stayed in the Louisiana business. They praise the article.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and the show credits play.
